title: Meeting Rooms II
directAnswer: The minimum number of rooms equals the maximum number of meetings happening at the same instant — the peak concurrency. Sort by start, keep a min-heap of the end times of meetings currently using a room; for each new meeting, if the earliest-ending room has freed up (its end ≤ new start) reuse it, otherwise allocate a new room. The heap's max size is the answer. O(n log n).

remember.pattern: Max concurrency via min-heap of end times (or chronological sweep)
remember.formula:
sort by start
heap = []  # end times of in-use rooms
for s, e in meetings:
    if heap and heap[0] <= s: heappop(heap)   # a room freed
    heappush(heap, e)
return len(heap)  # peak size
rules: **Rooms needed = peak number of simultaneously-active meetings.** Translate the whole problem to 'max overlap at any instant'.
Sort by **start**, and let the **min-heap hold end times** so the soonest-freeing room is always on top.
Reuse test is `heap.top() <= newStart` (with `<=`: a room freeing exactly when the next starts can be reused).
The answer is the **maximum** heap size reached (equivalently the final size if you only pop one per push) — track the peak.
Alternative: split into sorted starts[] and sorted ends[], sweep with two pointers; `room++` on a start before the next end, `room--` otherwise.
whenToUse: 'Minimum rooms / servers / machines to handle all intervals'
Maximum number of overlapping intervals at any point
Resource-allocation where each concurrent task needs its own unit
Peak-load / max-concurrency questions on time ranges
antiSignals: 'Can ONE person attend all?' → boolean adjacent-overlap check (LC 252)
'Merge the overlaps' → sort by start, sweep-merge (LC 56)
'Remove fewest to make disjoint' → greedy by end (LC 435)
You need WHICH room each meeting uses, not just the count → assign heap entries to room ids
remember.takeaway: Minimum rooms = maximum concurrent meetings — reframing 'allocation' as 'peak overlap' is the unlock. A min-heap of end times tells you in O(log n) whether any room has freed up; the chronological two-array sweep computes the same peak as a running +1/−1 balance.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reframe 'minimum rooms' as 'maximum simultaneous meetings' and use a min-heap of end times (or a sweep) to track peak concurrency, instead of trying to merge or pair-check.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to merge intervals (that counts disjoint groups, not concurrency), or comparing the new meeting against the wrong room — you must check the room that frees EARLIEST, which is exactly the heap top.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State 'rooms = peak overlap' upfront, justify the min-heap as 'the soonest-available room', use <= for back-to-back reuse, and offer the two-pointer sweep over sorted start/end arrays as an equivalent O(n log n) with a cleaner constant.

problemStatement:
Given an array of meeting time intervals `intervals` where `intervals[i] = [startᵢ, endᵢ]`, return the **minimum number of conference rooms required** so that all meetings can be held.

A room can be reused once a meeting finishes: a meeting ending at time `t` frees its room for another meeting starting at time `t` (back-to-back is allowed).
constraints: A room can be reused starting exactly at the time the previous meeting ended
understanding: You're scheduling meetings into rooms. Two meetings that overlap in time can't share a room, so at the busiest instant you need as many rooms as there are meetings running at once. Find that peak — that's the minimum number of rooms.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a room be reused the moment a meeting ends?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a meeting ending at t and one starting at t can share a room. So the 'is a room free?' test uses <= (end ≤ newStart).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. I'll sort by start (and for the sweep, also have ends sorted) — ordering by time is what makes this tractable.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the count of rooms or an assignment of meetings to rooms?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the minimum count. The heap naturally yields it as the peak number of rooms in use.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are meeting times integers and bounded?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — small enough that sorting is the bottleneck; no need for a coordinate-compression trick.

examples.explanation: [0,30] overlaps both [5,10] and [15,20], but those two don't overlap each other. Peak concurrency is 2 (during [5,10] and during [15,20], [0,30] is also running).
They don't overlap, so one room suffices — the second meeting reuses the room after the first.
All three are simultaneously active around time 3–5, so peak concurrency is 3.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree for interval-scheduling questions. Meeting Rooms II is the 'how many resources / peak overlap' branch — heap of end times or a chronological sweep.

approaches.name: Min-Heap of End Times
approaches.whenToMention: The most intuitive optimal — say 'a min-heap of end times is my pool of in-use rooms; the top is the one that frees soonest'.
hints: Reframe: the number of rooms you need is the largest number of meetings overlapping at any single moment. How do you track that as you scan in time order?
Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of the end times of meetings currently occupying rooms.
For each new meeting, if the smallest end time in the heap is ≤ its start, a room freed — pop it. Always push the new end. The heap size is the rooms in use; its peak is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n); each meeting does O(log n) heap work (one push, at most one pop), so the scan is O(n log n). The heap holds at most n end times → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the meetings by start time, then process them in that order while maintaining a min-heap of the end times of meetings that currently hold a room.

**Why a min-heap of end times.** When a new meeting starts, the only question is: *has any room freed up by now?* The room that frees the earliest is the one whose meeting ends soonest — exactly the minimum end time. A min-heap keyed on end time keeps that value on top in O(1), and removing it is O(log n). So for each meeting we peek the top: if `heap.top() <= newStart`, that room is free, pop it (we'll immediately reuse it). Then push the current meeting's end time regardless. If no room was free, we didn't pop, so the heap grew — that's a newly allocated room.

**Why the heap size IS the room count.** Every element in the heap is a meeting currently occupying a room. We pop at most one per step (a single room frees per arriving meeting in this formulation) and push exactly one, so the heap size at any moment equals the number of rooms in use at that time. The maximum it ever reaches is the peak concurrency — the minimum rooms required.

**Why `<=` and not `<` for reuse.** A room frees the instant its meeting ends. If the previous meeting ends exactly when the new one starts, the room is available — back-to-back is allowed — so the reuse condition is `end <= newStart`.
approaches.insight: The heap is a live 'pool of busy rooms', and the min-heap discipline means you always test against the room that becomes available first — testing any other room would be strictly worse. This 'keep the resource that frees soonest on top' idea is the heart of countless scheduling problems (CPU task scheduling, k-way merge, Single-Threaded CPU). Once 'min rooms = peak overlap' clicks, the heap is just the bookkeeping.

dryRun.intro: Heap holds end times of in-use rooms. Pop if the soonest-freeing room is free (top ≤ start), then push the new end.

code.python:
import heapq

def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0])
    heap: list[int] = []
    peak = 0
    for s, e in intervals:
        if heap and heap[0] <= s:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        heapq.heappush(heap, e)
        peak = max(peak, len(heap))
    return peak

java.explanation: Process meetings in start order so the heap reflects what's running 'now'.
Soonest-freeing room's end ≤ this start → that room is free, reuse it.
This meeting now occupies a room (reused or new) until its end time.
Rooms in use right now = heap size; the running max is the answer.

python.explanation: Start order lets the heap model the set of currently-active meetings.
heap[0] is the earliest end; ≤ start means a room freed (back-to-back allowed).
Add this meeting's end; if nothing was popped, the heap grew = new room.
Track peak concurrency = minimum rooms required.

diagrams.title: Heap of end times as meetings arrive
diagrams.caption: Each frame shows the heap (in-use room end times) after processing a start-sorted meeting. Heap size = rooms in use.

edgeCases.behavior: No top ever ≤ next start, so we push without popping each time → heap grows to 3 → returns 3.
Second meeting: top 30 ≤ 30 → reuse the room → heap size stays 1 → returns 1.

pitfalls: Using a max-heap or a heap of starts — you must surface the SOONEST-freeing room (min end).
Using `<` for reuse — a room freeing exactly at the new start should be reusable, so use `<=`.
Reporting the final heap size without tracking the peak (works in this one-pop-per-push form, but track peak to be safe).

approaches.name: Chronological Sweep — Two Sorted Arrays (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Offer as the slick alternative: 'separate starts and ends, sort each, and sweep a running room counter'.
hints: Forget about which room — just track how the count of active meetings rises and falls over time.
Split the intervals into a sorted array of start times and a sorted array of end times.
Walk both with two pointers: if the next start is before the next end, a meeting begins (rooms++); otherwise one ended (rooms--, advance the end pointer). Track the max rooms.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two sorts of n elements are O(n log n) and dominate; the two-pointer sweep is O(n). Two arrays of size n → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Decouple starts from ends. Build two arrays — all start times sorted, and all end times sorted — then sweep through time with two pointers.

**The +1/−1 mental model.** Picture walking a timeline. Every meeting start is a `+1` event (a room becomes occupied); every meeting end is a `−1` event (a room frees). The number of rooms in use at any instant is the running sum of these events in chronological order, and the answer is the maximum that running sum ever reaches. We don't need to know *which* meeting started or ended — only the net concurrency.

**Why two sorted arrays and not paired intervals.** A start and an end are independent events on the timeline, so we sort them independently. The start pointer `s` and end pointer `e` always point at the next upcoming start and next upcoming end. Compare them: if `starts[s] < ends[e]`, the next thing to happen is a meeting beginning, so `rooms++` and advance `s`. Otherwise the next thing is a meeting ending (or a simultaneous end that frees a room for the start), so `rooms--` and advance `e`. Track `max(rooms)`.

**Why `starts[s] < ends[e]` with strict `<`.** When a start and an end coincide (`start == end`), the room frees exactly as the new meeting begins — back-to-back reuse — so we should treat it as an end first (no new room). Strict `<` on the start side does exactly that: ties fall through to the `else` branch and decrement, letting the freed room be reused.

**Why this is the clean optimal.** Same O(n log n) as the heap, but the inner loop is just integer comparisons and increments — no heap operations, smaller constant, and arguably the easiest to get right once you see the +1/−1 framing.
approaches.insight: This is the sweep-line technique in its purest form: replace objects (intervals) with their boundary events (+1 starts, −1 ends), sort the events, and the running balance is your live quantity of interest — here, rooms in use. The heap and the sweep compute the identical peak; the sweep just makes 'peak overlap' literal. Recognizing 'max running balance over sorted events' generalizes to car-pooling, my-calendar, and CPU-load problems.

dryRun.intro: starts = [0,5,15], ends = [10,20,30]. Compare next start vs next end; +1 on a start, −1 on an end.

code.python:
def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    starts = sorted(iv[0] for iv in intervals)
    ends = sorted(iv[1] for iv in intervals)
    rooms = peak = 0
    e = 0
    for s in starts:
        while ends[e] <= s:
            rooms -= 1
            e += 1
        rooms += 1
        peak = max(peak, rooms)
    return peak

java.explanation: Starts and ends are independent timeline events, sorted separately.
Every meeting that ended at or before this start frees a room first (<= = back-to-back reuse).
Each freed meeting releases a room before we seat the new one.
This start occupies a room; peak of `rooms` over time is the answer.

python.line: starts = sorted(iv[0] for iv in intervals)
python.explanation: Sorted start events for the +1 side of the sweep.
Free every room whose meeting ended by time s (<= allows immediate reuse).
Seat the current meeting; track the running maximum as peak concurrency.

diagrams.title: Sweep over sorted start times
diagrams.caption: starts on top, with rooms balance updating. Each start frees any ended meetings first, then takes a room.

edgeCases.behavior: starts=[2,7], ends=[4,10]. start 2 → rooms 1; start 7: end 4 ≤ 7 frees → rooms 0 then 1 → peak 1.
No end ≤ the next start until all three are seated → rooms climbs 1→2→3 → peak 3.

pitfalls: Pairing starts with their own ends — they must be sorted independently as separate event streams.
Using `<` instead of `<=` when freeing rooms — would refuse back-to-back reuse and overcount rooms.
Returning the final `rooms` instead of the running peak — the max can occur mid-sweep.

commonMistakes: Merging intervals and counting groups — that counts disjoint clusters, not peak concurrency.
Comparing a new meeting to an arbitrary room instead of the soonest-freeing one (heap top).
Using strict < for room reuse, refusing back-to-back meetings that should share a room.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Merging intervals instead of counting overlap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Merge Intervals collapses overlapping ranges into groups, but a single merged group can contain 3 simultaneous meetings. The room count is peak concurrency, not the number of merged groups.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
merged = merge(intervals)
return len(merged)            # counts clusters, not concurrency

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing against the wrong room
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only the room that frees EARLIEST matters — if even that one is still busy, every room is busy and you need a new one. That's why the min-heap top (smallest end) is the right thing to test.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
// checks the most-recently-added end, not the soonest-freeing
if (lastEnd <= iv[0]) reuseRoom();
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (!heap.isEmpty() && heap.peek() <= iv[0]) heap.poll(); // soonest-freeing
heap.offer(iv[1]);

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict inequality blocks back-to-back reuse
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A room freeing exactly when the next meeting starts can be reused. Using < instead of <= forces an unnecessary extra room when end == newStart.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if heap and heap[0] < s:      # refuses reuse at end == start
    heapq.heappop(heap)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if heap and heap[0] <= s:     # back-to-back reuse allowed
    heapq.heappop(heap)
